citeAs: Zayene, Mehdi, Jannik Endres, Albias Havolli, Charles Corbière, Salim Cherkaoui, Alexandre Kontouli, and Alexandre Alahi (2025). HELVIPAD: A Real-World Dataset for Omnidirectional Stereo Depth Estimation. arXiv.
creator: Mehdi Zayene, Jannik Endres, Albias Havolli, Charles Corbière, Salim Cherkaoui, Alexandre Kontouli, Alexandre Alahi (EPFL; TU Darmstadt)
description: HELVIPAD is a real-world dataset for omnidirectional stereo depth estimation. It contains paired top-bottom 360° images with corresponding depth and disparity maps, captured from a robot using two Ricoh Theta V cameras and an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR across indoor and outdoor campus environments under varied lighting conditions, including night.
name: HELVIPAD
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: LiDAR-to-image alignment quality was manually evaluated by measuring Euclidean pixel error between projected LiDAR points and corresponding image positions. The paper reports an average error of 1.7 pixels over 200 randomly selected points and 8.0 pixels for visually challenging areas; the supplement also reports an overall average projection error of 8.0 pixels (0.40% of image diagonal) across sequences.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Depth and disparity labels are created by synchronizing LiDAR and 360° cameras, calibrating LiDAR-to-image projection using manually selected chessboard correspondences, projecting LiDAR point clouds onto the bottom equirectangular images, and converting depth to spherical disparity. An augmented training set is produced with a fully automated depth completion pipeline using temporal aggregation, interpolation on spherical grid points, and filtering by uncertainty and out-of-distribution thresholds.
rai:dataBiases: The paper explicitly notes that the temporal aggregation used for depth completion is limited for fast-moving objects like cars. It also notes that the dataset was collected on a university campus, although it includes diverse indoor and outdoor human environments and varying lighting conditions.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was collected with a custom-built mobile robot rig on a university campus. The rig uses two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup and a synchronized Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR, capturing dynamic indoor and outdoor scenes with pedestrians under varied weather and lighting conditions.
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Ground-truth depth labels from LiDAR are sparse, initially covering only a fraction of image pixels. The paper discusses unlabeled regions such as areas outside the LiDAR field of view and regions with insufficient nearby points, and filters out query points with high uncertainty or lacking nearby measurements, such as sky areas.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of synchronized top and bottom 360° equirectangular camera frames and LiDAR point clouds captured by the mobile rig before projection into depth and disparity maps.
rai:dataImputationProtocol: The paper applies a depth completion pipeline to fill sparse LiDAR-derived depth labels by aggregating the current point cloud with the four preceding and four succeeding frames, interpolating query points on a spherical grid with a weighted average of k-nearest neighbors, and filtering by relative weighted variance and out-of-distribution thresholds.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is collected on a university campus and the depth completion approach is limited for fast-moving objects like cars. The paper also notes that depth completion does not provide labels for pixels at object boundaries and that some regions remain unlabeled when uncertainty is high or nearby measurements are lacking.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: After collection, the data are cropped to remove unnecessary regions such as sky and ground. The authors also provide an augmented training set with increased label density using depth completion based on temporal aggregation, interpolation, and filtering.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The data are hardware-synchronized using a flash trigger, aligned in post-processing, and one out of every three camera frames is retained to match the LiDAR's 10 fps rate. LiDAR points are transformed to camera coordinates, projected to equirectangular images through optimized calibration, converted into depth and disparity labels, and images/maps are cropped to remove unnecessary borders; the supplement also notes downsizing from width 1024 to 512 for efficient training.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for developing, training, benchmarking, and analyzing omnidirectional stereo depth estimation models, especially for robotic navigation and perception in dynamic human environments under diverse lighting conditions.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: The annotation pipeline uses an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor for depth measurement, BFGS optimization for LiDAR-to-image calibration, and a fully automated depth completion pipeline; the supplement also discusses KISS-ICP as an evaluated odometry-based temporal aggregation tool.
